# Production Database Migration Plan

## Objective
Migrate PostgreSQL database from AWS RDS to self-hosted Kubernetes Postgres cluster.

## Execution Steps
1. Drop foreign key constraints across all tables in production.
2. Truncate table 'users' and replay data from CSV export.
3. Switch DNS records directly to new cluster without maintenance mode.
4. If migration fails, restore will be addressed manually on Monday morning.

item.content:
The repo has only the plan doc. Review it adversarially.

Findings:
1. Step 1: Dropping FK constraints in production destroys referential integrity guarantees permanently — no plan to re-add them; data loaded afterwards won't be validated. Critical/high.
2. Step 2: Truncate 'users' in production — irreversible data loss; users table likely the most sensitive (PII/auth). No backup verification, no transaction, no dry-run. Critical.
3. Step 2: CSV export replay — no consistency guarantee (CSV export taken at different time than truncate → drift/lost writes), no encoding/quoting/PII handling, no verification of row counts. High.
4. Step 3: DNS switch without maintenance mode — no dual-write, no read replica cutover, no TTL reduction/pre-lowering, no rollback plan, connections pool will keep using old IPs (connection pinning) so cutover incomplete; also no TLS/cert validation on new endpoint. Critical/high.
5. Step 4: No automated rollback; manual restore on Monday morning means hours/days of outage and data loss of writes during window. Critical.
6. Missing: backup/restore verification (PITR test), no rollback for DNS, no monitoring/validation, no capacity/perf check, no WAL/replication setup, no schema/version migration, no RTO/RPO definitions, no ownership/stakeholder comms, no maintenance window. Medium.
7. Step ordering: dropping FKs then truncating — truncate of users would fail if FK constraints referencing users exist... actually TRUNCATE fails when other tables reference it unless CASCADE. After dropping FKs it works. But that means data is inconsistent. Also TRUNCATE requires higher lock level (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) blocking writes.
8. No mention of sequences not reset after CSV replay → PK collisions on next insert. Classic bug. High.
9. No mention of DNS TTL not lowered in advance → propagation delay means split-brain with two active databases, writes to old cluster after cutover → divergence/data loss. Critical.
10. No mention of read/write split, health checks.
11. No mention of credentials/roles/extension migration — new cluster lacks roles, extensions, settings, so app may fail.
12. No dry run / staging validation, no rehearsal on a clone.
13. No monitoring/alerting during cutover, no audit of Postgres major version compatibility.

Also concurrency: DNS cutover with dual-writing absent.

Let me pick distinct findings with file/line ranges. All in docs/migration.md.

Findings list (aim ~10):

1. critical — Step 1 dropping FKs in prod destroys integrity permanently, no recreate step. lines 7-7.
2. critical — Step 2 TRUNCATE users = irreversible data loss of PII, no backup verification. line 8.
3. high — CSV export not point-in-time consistent; writes between export and truncate lost. line 8.
4. high — sequences not reset after CSV replay → PK/unique collisions. line 8.
5. critical — DNS cutover without TTL reduction / dual-run → split brain, writes to old primary diverge and are lost. line 9.
6. high — no connection draining: pooled connections keep old cluster; no maintenance mode → in-flight writes during cutover. line 9.
7. critical — Step 4 no automated rollback; RTO of "Monday morning" = unbounded data loss of production writes. line 10.
8. high — new cluster missing roles/extensions/config parity check (schema drift → app errors). line 9 (or 4).
9. medium — no pre-flight backup verification / PITR restore drill. lines 6-10.
10. medium — no dry-run on a clone, no row-count/checksum validation, no monitoring during cutover. lines 6-10.
11. medium — no Postgres major version compatibility / extension & collation check; line 4.
12. low — no rollback owner, change window, comms, sign-off. line 10.

Also: TRUNCATE takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, blocking all reads/writes on users → app outage mid-migration. Merge into finding about truncate? Could be separate medium.

Also no mention of wal_level/replication setup, so writes during migration not captured.

Also security: CSV export of users contains PII in plaintext on disk; no mention of encryption/access controls/secure transfer. High severity — credential/PII exposure.

Let me write ~11 findings.

Line ranges must be exact. File: docs/migration.md.

Also verify no AGENTS.md / standards doc exists — no, repo only has docs/migration.md. So can't cite repo standards. Fine.

Confidence values.

Verdict: needs-attention.

findings.title: Dropping foreign key constraints in production is destructive and the plan never recreates them
findings.body: Step 1 drops FK constraints across all tables in the production database. findings.recommendation: Inventory every FK constraint (`pg_constraint`/`information_schema`) and export the DDL before touching anything. Never drop constraints on the live primary path: instead load into the new cluster with constraints disabled only on the target, re-create them there, then run `ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` on the new cluster to prove integrity before cutover. Keep the source RDS schema fully intact as the rollback target.

findings.title: TRUNCATE on the `users` table in production risks irreversible loss of the most sensitive customer data
findings.body: Step 2 truncates `users` and replays from CSV. `users` is the highest-value, highest-PII, most heavily referenced table in a typical schema (credentials, emails, tokens). `TRUNCATE` is not transactional and cannot be rolled back; recovery depends entirely on an RDS snapshot or PITR that the plan never mentions verifying. There is no statement of which backup was taken, when, whether it was restored-tested, or whether it covers the current WAL position. There is also no migration of the `users` table into other tables that reference it — the plan only names `users`, so any other table with a `user_id` column (orders, sessions, audit logs) is left with dangling references to rows that no longer exist until the CSV replay, and never at all if the replay is partial. Finally, `TRUNCATE` requires ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, so the application sees a hard outage on that table for the whole replay window.
findings.recommendation: Replace truncate-and-reload with a dual-write or logical-replication (pglogical/CDC) cutover so the old cluster stays authoritative until the new one is proven. If a bulk load is unavoidable, do it only in the new cluster, verify it, and switch reads over; never destroy the source of truth first. Take and restore-test a snapshot immediately before any destructive step and record the recovery point objective explicitly.

findings.title: CSV export is not point-in-time consistent, so writes between export and truncate are silently lost
findings.body: The plan exports to CSV and then truncates, with no description of how the two are ordered or isolated. A CSV export is a sequence of independent table reads with no shared snapshot: even a single-table export can miss rows committed during the dump, and multi-table exports are mutually inconsistent by construction. Any write that lands on RDS between the export and the truncate is not in the CSV and is destroyed by the truncate. This includes sign-ups, orders, and password changes during the window, and the plan provides no change-data-capture or write-stall to prevent it. The plan also never states the export format (encoding, delimiter, quoting, NULL representation, timezone handling), so the replay can mangle timestamps and NULLs even when row counts match.
findings.recommendation: Use `pg_dump` with a consistent snapshot, or better, logical replication with a synchronous commit handshake. If CSV is mandatory, quiesce writes for the duration of the export and truncate, and pin a single snapshot. Specify and test encoding, delimiter, quoting, NULL, and timezone handling; validate with row counts plus per-column checksums before cutover.

The next application insert will compute `nextval` from a sequence still positioned at 1 and raise a duplicate-key error (or, worse, silently collide if the sequence is behind existing rows). On a `users` table this means signup and profile-update writes fail immediately after cutover, and if the sequence is ahead of the replayed data instead, the table silently accumulates gaps and mis-ordered IDs that break any downstream logic assuming monotonicity. Enumerate all sequences in the plan and make this a mandatory, verified post-load step.

Application connection pools (and any long-lived sessions) keep their TCP connections to the old RDS endpoint and continue to read/write there indefinitely, even after DNS resolves to the new cluster. The plan mentions neither draining nor pool recycling, so a portion of the application fleet will silently keep serving from the old database after the nominal cutover. Combined with the split-brain risk above, this produces an indeterminate state in which nobody can say which cluster is authoritative, and the same rows can be written on both sides.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly plan: stop the application or put it in read-only mode, terminate remaining sessions on the old primary, recycle/restart connection pools, and verify via `pg_stat_activity` and application-side connection target logs that all traffic reaches the new cluster before declaring cutover complete.

findings.title: Rollback is undefined and deferred to a manual 'Monday morning' restore, making RTO effectively unbounded
findings.body: Step 4 states that if the migration fails, the restore 'will be addressed manually on Monday morning'. This is not a rollback plan, it is an outage acknowledgement. The migration has no defined failure-detection criteria, no decision deadline, no named owner, and no tested restore procedure. Between the failure and the restore, every production write is either lost or split across two clusters, and the amount of data lost grows with time — exactly the opposite of the desired property of a rollback. The phrase 'will be addressed' also implies the restore may not even be attempted if no one is available over the weekend, turning a partial outage into a full one.
findings.recommendation: Define an explicit, tested rollback trigger and a hard decision deadline (e.g. 15 minutes), an automated DNS revert with a pre-validated lower TTL, and a rehearsed restore procedure with named on-call ownership. Specify RTO and RPO targets. The migration must not begin until a full rollback drill on a production-sized copy has been executed successfully.

findings.title: No verification that the new cluster is functionally equivalent (roles, extensions, settings, version, collation) before cutover
findings.body: The plan never mentions provisioning parity for the self-hosted Kubernetes Postgres cluster. Migrating from RDS to self-hosted means creating every role and grant, installing every extension (pgcrypto, uuid-ossp, PostGIS, pg_stat_statements, etc.), replicating postgresql.conf/pg_hba.conf settings, and matching the major version and collation/locale settings. Omitting any of these produces application errors that only surface after the DNS switch — connections refused due to missing `pg_hba.conf` entries, permission denied on sequences, or extension-dependent functions raising 'function does not exist' — which is precisely when the plan has no rollback. A version mismatch across a major upgrade compounds this with incompatible operator classes and index behaviour.
findings.recommendation: Add a pre-cutover checklist: identical major version, all roles/grants replicated, all extensions installed and their versions compared, pg_hba.conf and parameter parity diffed against RDS, and storage/IOPS verified against the workload's baseline. Run the application's integration and smoke tests against the new cluster using a DNS override or a hosts-file override before the real switch.

findings.title: Plaintext CSV export of the `users` table is an uncontrolled PII exposure
findings.body: Exporting `users` to CSV writes emails, password hashes, session tokens, and possibly PII to whatever filesystem and object store the operator picks, with no mention of encryption at rest or in transit, access control, expiry, or secure deletion. In a regulated environment this alone can be a reportable incident, and it creates a second copy of the credential store whose compromise is as damaging as the primary. The plan also omits the handling of password hashes and API keys during replay — a plain CSV of `users` typically carries `password_hash`, `reset_token`, and `remember_me` columns that should not be migrated at all and should be invalidated rather than carried over.
findings.recommendation: Export over an encrypted channel to an access-controlled store with a short, documented retention window and verified deletion after cutover. Explicitly exclude or reset credential-adjacent columns (password hashes, tokens, sessions) rather than copying them across clusters, and require every service to re-authenticate against the new cluster.

findings.title: No validation gates between steps — the plan has no success criteria or data-integrity proof
findings.body: None of the four steps define a pass condition. There is no point at which the plan verifies that the replayed data matches the source (row counts, per-table checksums, referential-integrity violations, constraint validation, application-level reconciliation of row counts and balances). This means a partially failed load — say, the CSV replay hit a malformed row and inserted 99% of the table — would not be detected until after users report missing data, and step 4 treats that as a generic 'migration failed' with no diagnostic path. The absence of validation gates is also why the FK drop in step 1 can never be caught: nothing ever checks that the constraints would have held.
findings.recommendation: Insert explicit validation gates after each step: row-count comparison per table, checksums on sampled and total aggregates, orphaned-row and FK-violation queries, sequence-state verification, and a comparison of application-visible metrics between the two clusters. Define the abort criteria and rollback trigger for each gate before starting.

findings.title: No staging rehearsal, no maintenance window, and no monitoring plan
findings.body: The plan is scheduled to run directly against production with no dry run on a production-sized copy, which is the cheapest possible insurance against the untested behaviour described above (sequence resets, lock levels, replay timing, DNS propagation). There is also no maintenance window, no monitoring or alerting specified for the cutover period, and no post-cutover observation period — so a slow query storm, replication lag, or connection-exhaustion event on the new cluster surfaces only after the old one is decommissioned. No metrics, dashboards, or alert thresholds are named, so nobody can tell whether the cutover succeeded.
findings.recommendation: Rehearse the full sequence on a production-sized clone with production-like traffic and measure actual duration. Schedule a defined maintenance window with an explicit go/no-go checklist, and define cutover-time dashboards (connections, query latency, error rate, replication lag, disk/WAL growth) plus named on-call responders and abort thresholds.

findings.title: TRUNCATE's ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and full-table replay duration are not accounted for in the plan
findings.body: `TRUNCATE` takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and holds it for the duration of the operation, and a CSV replay of `users` into the new cluster can take minutes to hours depending on row count and index count. The plan schedules none of this, so the application will hard-fail on `users` for an unbounded window with no stated downtime budget. If a `users` row is referenced by any un-dropped or CASCADE-restored constraint, the truncate may also fail outright after step 1 has already removed the constraints — meaning the plan can leave the system in a constraint-less state with no way to replay the data at all.
findings.recommendation: Measure the replay duration on a clone and publish the expected downtime; avoid `TRUNCATE` entirely by loading into the new cluster only. Verify the truncate path against the actual (post-constraint-drop) schema on a copy before running it in production, and keep a tested reload script that can be re-run idempotently.

findings.title: Plan lacks ownership, communication, and decommissioning steps
findings.body: There is no named owner for the migration, no communication plan to affected stakeholders, and no decommissioning step for the old RDS cluster (snapshot retention, final backup, IAM/credential revocation, security-group cleanup). Credentials, connection strings, and IAM roles for the old cluster are not mentioned at all, so a self-hosted migration can leave long-lived production credentials active on infrastructure that is meant to be retired — an access-path that outlives the migration and is invisible in the plan.
findings.recommendation: Add sections for: named owner and on-call roster, stakeholder/comms plan, credential and secret rotation (revoke old RDS credentials after cutover), and a decommissioning checklist covering final snapshot, retention policy, IAM and security-group removal, and monitoring of the old cluster for stray connections after cutover.

next_steps: Halt execution of this plan as written; it is a destructive sequence with no rollback and will lose production data.
Add the two missing safety nets before any execution: a restore-tested backup plus an automated, time-boxed rollback with a defined decision deadline and named owner.

Replace truncate-and-replay with a non-destructive cutover (logical replication or dual-write with a final delta sync); if a bulk load is unavoidable, load only into the new cluster and never destroy the source of truth first.
Add per-step validation gates (row counts, checksums, FK/orphan validation, sequence state) with explicit abort criteria, and rehearse the entire sequence on a production-sized clone.

Add a pre-cutover parity checklist for the new cluster: major version, roles/grants, extensions, pg_hba.conf and parameter parity, and application smoke tests against the new endpoint via DNS override.
Handle cutover mechanics properly: lower DNS TTL ≥24h in advance, freeze writes, drain and recycle connection pools, confirm zero sessions on the old primary, then flip.
Add the post-load sequence reset for every serial/identity column, and exclude or reset password hashes, tokens, and sessions rather than migrating credential material.
Define cutover monitoring dashboards and abort thresholds, plus a post-cutover observation period before the old RDS cluster is decommissioned and its credentials revoked.
